facts.text: I rewrote the provided content as a SaaS product marketing piece with a title.
The Olmsted County planning department in Minnesota was consolidated with the city of Rochester under a single Accela agency from November 2007 until March 2021.
In March 2021, Olmsted County employed its own Accela agency.
Olmsted County used Accela Citizen Access with Viewable Data and Online Inspections.
Olmsted County had a low-value Laserfiche connection because documents were housed in the city of Rochester’s servers.
Employees were double-inputting information into various systems.
Olmsted County hosted Laserfiche data on the city of Rochester’s servers rather than saving it in a permanent archival location.
Olmsted County did not have a reliable backup in the event of a natural disaster or catastrophic server crash.
Citizens were confused about which jurisdiction to designate during city planning processes because two local governments were using one site.
The payment adapter was not accepting payments to Olmsted County and the city of Rochester.
The payment adapter only allowed payments to Rochester.
Olmsted County did not have control of automation for emails, reports, analytics dashboards, and training.
Olmsted County did not have complete access to users and licenses.
Olmsted County required software integrations to Tyler Tax System / iasWorld v2020.1.43.
Olmsted County required software integrations to iNovah Cashier v2.60.189.6.
Olmsted County required software integrations to GIS XAPO (new address parcel owner system Laserfiche v10.4).
The system involved ten steps with 14 sub-steps for processing paper and data.
Sometimes Olmsted County staff refused to process the data, leaving scanning to be done at the end by the administrative team.
Olmsted County needed to upgrade and streamline computer and software systems to meet public needs better.
Olmsted County needed professional assistance in planning and conducting software integrations.
Olmsted County aimed to provide a single system for inputting data to save workers’ time.
Olmsted County aimed to integrate Laserfiche and Accela and other systems while optimizing the county’s systems for Accela.
Olmsted County aimed to reduce paper and data processing substeps in a cumbersome system involving 24 steps and substeps.
Olmsted County aimed to enable citizens to submit applications online instead of using surface mail or visiting county offices.
Olmsted County aimed to enable a safe and straightforward way for citizens to make online payments.
The document states that the online payment need was especially important during the COVID-19 era.
During COVID-19 lockdowns, allowing people to do as much business as possible online with government became more important.
The solution was to integrate the Laserfiche connector and Accela connector with the mentioned systems to increase automation, employee productivity, and efficiency.
The solution enabled Olmsted County to offer online payments to its citizens.
After implementation, employees reduced time spent on file management by 90%.
After implementation, workers no longer had to manually search for metadata from property records and save documents in as many as 3 to 4 locations.
After implementation, there was no need for staff to input the same data twice into different systems.
After implementation, the county did not need to worry about staff members missing or skipping steps in vital processes.
Olmsted County resolved 12 of 24 sub-steps for paper and data processing.
The integration resolved some 50% of process substeps with Accela–Laserfiche integration.
Olmsted County citizens could submit plumbing and mechanical applications online.
Olmsted County citizens could submit new well applications online.
Olmsted County citizens could submit new septic applications online.
Olmsted County citizens could use online inspections.
With the new integrations, 53% of trade permits were submitted online.
With the new integrations, 66% of new good permits were done online.
Citizens in Olmsted could make payments online with credit cards and Echeck.
Approximately 46% of individuals who made online payments during the previous four months started their application process.
The case describes how local governments can better serve their community by deploying state-of-the-art payment and document processing systems.
The case states that streamlining processes saves government workers time and effort.
The case states that citizens can submit applications before doing new work such as mechanical or plumbing or installing a new well.
The case states that citizens can focus on projects instead of dealing with additional paperwork or visits to Olmsted County offices.
